questions.stem: An app is shipped only as a 64-bit installer. The user's PC is running 32-bit Windows. What happens?

choices.text: It installs and runs fine, since 32-bit is backwards compatible
It will not run; a 32-bit OS cannot run 64-bit software
It installs but is limited to 4 GB of RAM
It runs only after enabling Hyper-V

questions.explanation: A 32-bit OS cannot execute 64-bit binaries. The compatibility goes the other way: 64-bit Windows runs both 32 and 64-bit apps.
questions.trap: It's tempting to think 'backwards compatible' both ways, but the bridge only runs in the 64-bit-running-32-bit direction.

questions.stem: Older 32-bit applications installed on 64-bit Windows are placed into which folder by default?

choices.text: C:\Program Files (x86)
C:\Program Files
C:\Windows\System32
C:\Users\Public

questions.explanation: 32-bit applications on 64-bit Windows install to 'C:\Program Files (x86)'. The 'x86' suffix is the giveaway.
questions.trap: Confusingly, System32 actually holds 64-bit system files on 64-bit Windows. The 32-bit versions live in SysWOW64.

questions.stem: A graphic designer plans to install 3D modeling software with heavy rendering. Which graphics setup is appropriate?

choices.text: Integrated graphics built into the CPU
No graphics card at all; CPU rendering only
A dedicated graphics card with its own VRAM
A removable USB graphics adapter

questions.explanation: Demanding software like 3D modeling or video editing needs a dedicated GPU with its own VRAM (video RAM). Integrated graphics share CPU memory and are too slow.
questions.trap: Integrated graphics handle basic tasks fine but choke on 3D workloads.

questions.stem: An expensive specialized application refuses to launch unless a specific physical USB device is plugged in. What is this licensing mechanism called?

choices.text: A network license server
An ISO image
An EULA prompt
A hardware token (dongle)

questions.explanation: A hardware token (often a USB dongle) is a physical key required for the application to run. It is a strong form of license control on niche professional software.
questions.trap: A license server is software-based; the question specifies a physical USB device.

questions.stem: An application's documented RAM requirement is '8 GB minimum'. What does this number include?

choices.text: RAM for the OS, this app, and all other running apps
RAM for the app itself only - it does NOT include what the OS is already using
Only the VRAM on the GPU
The recommended swap file size

questions.explanation: Published RAM requirements list what the app needs above and beyond the OS. The user must have enough RAM left after the OS overhead.
questions.trap: Treating the number as 'total RAM in the system' guarantees an under-provisioned machine.

questions.stem: An admin downloads a large ISO file for OS installation. What is an ISO, and how is it typically used?

choices.text: An archive of audio files; played back with a media player
A document format; opens in any word processor
A perfect digital copy of a disc; can be mounted so the OS treats it like a real drive
A driver bundle; installs via Device Manager

questions.explanation: An ISO is a perfect digital copy of a disc. You mount it and the OS reads it as if it were a real CD/DVD drive.
questions.trap: ISO is not an audio or document container; the name comes from the ISO 9660 disc filesystem.

questions.stem: When a user installs an application, what permission level does that application inherit?

choices.text: Always SYSTEM-level, regardless of who runs it
Only read permissions, never write or execute
Permissions defined by the EULA, separate from any user account
The exact same permissions as the user who installed it

questions.explanation: Apps inherit the installing user's permissions, including access to local files, network drives, and services.
questions.trap: Apps do not magically receive SYSTEM rights; if the installer ran as a standard user, the app is bounded to those rights.

questions.stem: A company is about to roll out a new line-of-business app to 500 employees. Before mass deployment, where is the safest place to test it?

choices.text: A sandbox environment
The CFO's laptop
Random workstations across the production network
Skip testing; ship straight to production

questions.explanation: A sandbox is an isolated environment where the app can be tested for compatibility and impact without risking the production network or live users.
questions.trap: Picking a real user's laptop creates business risk; the whole point of a sandbox is no impact to production.
